name: Virtue Epistemology
statement: Knowledge is true belief that manifests intellectual virtue, so evaluate the knower, not just the belief.
statementAccent: true belief that manifests intellectual virtue
meaning: Virtue epistemology is a family of contemporary approaches to the theory of knowledge that give intellectual, or epistemic, virtue a central and fundamental role, taking the epistemic agent and the agent's cognitive character or competences, rather than only properties of beliefs, as the primary focus of evaluation. Where traditional epistemology asks what makes a belief justified, virtue epistemology shifts attention to the knower, analyzing knowledge and justified belief in terms of the intellectual virtues the agent brings to bear. The field divides into two main strands. Virtue reliabilism, associated with Ernest Sosa and John Greco, treats the intellectual virtues as reliable cognitive faculties or competences, stable abilities such as perception, memory, and sound reasoning that reliably produce true beliefs; knowledge, on this view, is true belief that is creditable to the agent's competence. Sosa's influential framework analyzes a belief as a kind of performance assessable for accuracy, adroitness, and aptness, so that an apt belief is one that is accurate because adroit, true because it manifests the agent's competence. Virtue responsibilism, associated with Linda Zagzebski and Lorraine Code, instead treats the intellectual virtues as acquired character traits, such as open-mindedness, intellectual courage, conscientiousness, and thoroughness, analogous to the moral virtues. Virtue epistemology grew out of Ernest Sosa's work around 1980 and connects the theory of knowledge to virtue ethics.
mechanism: Virtue epistemology reorients the analysis of knowledge around the qualities of the knower. Instead of asking only whether a belief has the right relation to evidence, it asks whether the belief issues from the agent's intellectual virtues, and it uses that idea to explain knowledge, justification, and epistemic value. The reliabilist strand, developed by Ernest Sosa and John Greco, understands intellectual virtues as reliable cognitive competences, faculties like vision, memory, and inference that are stable and truth-conducive. Sosa organizes this with the AAA structure: a belief, as a performance aimed at truth, can be accurate if it hits the mark of truth, adroit if it manifests skill or competence, and apt if it is accurate because adroit, that is, true precisely because it manifests the agent's competence rather than luck. Knowledge is then apt belief, true belief creditable to the knower's competence, which reframes knowing as a cognitive achievement. The responsibilist strand, developed by Linda Zagzebski and Lorraine Code, models intellectual virtues on moral virtues, as praiseworthy character traits, open-mindedness, intellectual courage, fair-mindedness, conscientiousness, cultivated through effort and expressed in good inquiry. Both strands share the move from belief-evaluation to agent-evaluation. This lets virtue epistemology address the Gettier problem, by requiring that the belief's truth be attributable to virtue rather than luck, offer a way past the deadlock between foundationalism and coherentism that Sosa first pressed in 1980, and connect epistemology to the broader theory of the virtues.

examples.text: On Sosa's account a belief is apt, and so knowledge, when it is accurate because adroit, true because it manifests competence.
Virtue reliabilism treats virtues as reliable faculties like perception; virtue responsibilism treats them as character traits like open-mindedness.
Virtue epistemology reframes knowing as a cognitive achievement creditable to the knower, not mere true belief.

variants.name: Virtue reliabilism
variants.text: Sosa's and Greco's view that intellectual virtues are reliable cognitive competences and knowledge is apt belief.

variants.name: Virtue responsibilism
variants.text: Zagzebski's and Code's view that intellectual virtues are cultivated character traits analogous to moral virtues.

whyItMatters: Virtue epistemology is one of the most influential developments in the theory of knowledge over the past several decades, marking a shift of focus from the evaluation of beliefs to the evaluation of epistemic agents and their intellectual character. By making the intellectual virtues central, it offers fresh resources for old problems. It gives a natural response to the Gettier problem, treating knowledge as apt belief or as a cognitive achievement creditable to the knower's competence, so that lucky true beliefs are excluded because their truth does not manifest virtue. It promises a way past the long impasse between foundationalism and coherentism, which was Ernest Sosa's motivation in his 1980 paper The Raft and the Pyramid. And it reconnects epistemology with ethics, since the responsibilist tradition of Zagzebski and Code models intellectual virtues like open-mindedness and intellectual courage on the moral virtues, opening questions about intellectual character, education, and the cultivation of good thinkers. The framework has generated rich debate over whether apt belief truly captures knowledge, over cases like the fake barns, and over the value of knowledge.

working.text: shift from asking whether a belief is justified to asking whether it manifests the agent's intellectual virtue.
treat virtues as reliable competences, on virtue reliabilism, or as cultivated character traits, on virtue responsibilism.
count knowledge as apt belief, true because it manifests competence, excluding mere luck.

limits: Virtue epistemology faces significant objections, several concerning whether it fully solves the problems it targets. Duncan Pritchard and others argue that Sosa's apt-belief account gives the wrong verdict in fake-barn cases, where an agent forms a true belief by exercising a genuine perceptual competence yet, because the surrounding environment is full of barn facades that would have fooled them, the belief seems too lucky to count as knowledge even though it appears apt; such environmental luck suggests aptness may not be sufficient for knowledge. There is also the value problem, pressed by Linda Zagzebski, that an adequate account of knowledge must explain why knowledge is more valuable than mere true belief, a demand virtue accounts try but are not universally agreed to meet. The two strands, reliabilist and responsibilist, also pull in different directions about what an intellectual virtue is, a reliable faculty or an acquired character trait, and whether one framework can capture both everyday perceptual knowledge and the achievements of conscientious inquiry.
misreadings: Virtue epistemology is not the claim that knowing requires being a morally good person; its intellectual virtues are cognitive competences or intellectual character traits, not moral goodness as such. Its two strands differ: virtue reliabilism counts reliable faculties like perception as virtues, so it does not require reflectively cultivated character for all knowledge, while virtue responsibilism emphasizes such character. And apt belief is not uncontroversially sufficient for knowledge, given fake-barn and environmental-luck cases, so treating virtue epistemology as demanding moral virtue, as always requiring cultivated character, or as having definitively solved Gettier, misreads a major contemporary approach.
origin: A family of contemporary approaches, growing from Ernest Sosa's work around 1980, that make the intellectual virtues central to the analysis of knowledge, divided into virtue reliabilism and virtue responsibilism.
